Q: Inserting an image as background in PySimpleGUI window A:

If you want to do anything involving layered elements (eg a background image with text written over the top of it) directly in PSG/FSG, you'll probably need to use a Graph. Then you can place items where- and how-ever you want in the window, including (for example) a window-resolution sized image placed behind all other elements.

A quick example:

import FreeSimpleGUI  as sg

class sample():

    def __init__(self):

        self.bg_images = ["..\\Assets\\misc_images\\b+w_16.png", "..\\Assets\\misc_images\\Composite_contrast_w_invert_mask_bf564d.png", "..\\Assets\\misc_images\\combined_blank_4.png"]
        self.bg_figure_idx:int=0
        self.bg_figure_id:int=0 # the returned figure_ID
        self.current_image=self.bg_images[self.bg_figure_idx]

        self.window_size = (900,700)
        self.graph_bottom_left = (0,self.window_size[1])
        self.graph_top_right = (self.window_size[0],0)


    def change_background_image(self):

        sample_image = self.bg_images[self.bg_figure_idx]

        new_background_image = sg_graph.draw_image(filename=sample_image, location=(0,0))
        sg_graph.send_figure_to_back(new_background_image)
        sg_graph.delete_figure(self.bg_figure_id)
        self.bg_figure_id = new_background_image
        window.refresh()

        self.bg_figure_idx += 1
        if self.bg_figure_idx == len(self.bg_images):
            self.bg_figure_idx = 0

samp = sample()


def graph_list():
    graph = sg.Graph(samp.window_size, samp.graph_bottom_left, samp.graph_top_right, background_color="green", key="sg_graph", enable_events=True)
    return graph

def add_background_img(sg_graph:sg.Graph):

    sample_image = rf"..\\Assets\\misc_images\\Composite_contrast_w_invert_mask_bf564d.png"

    background_image = sg_graph.draw_image(filename=sample_image, location=(0,0))
    sg_graph.send_figure_to_back(background_image)
    samp.bg_figure_id = background_image
    sg_graph.draw_rectangle(top_left=(int(window.size[0]/2)-410, int(window.size[1]/2)-100), bottom_right=(int(window.size[0]/2)+410, int(window.size[1]/2)+100), fill_color="grey", line_color="black", line_width=4)
    centre = int(window.size[0]/2), int(window.size[1]/2)
    sg_graph.draw_text(text="THERE ARE WORDS HERE.", location=centre, font="courier 40 bold underline", color="white")
    sg_graph.draw_text(text="THERE ARE WORDS HERE ", location=centre, font="courier 40 underline", color="black")

    window.refresh()


window = sg.Window(title="background_image", layout=[[graph_list()]], size=samp.window_size, resizable=True, background_color="black", finalize=True, margins=(0,0), element_padding=0)

sg_graph = window["sg_graph"] # type:sg.Graph
window.timer_start(3000, key="change_background")
add_background_img(sg_graph)

while True and not window.is_closed():
    event, values = window.read(500)

    if event == "change_background":
        samp.change_background_image()

Q: Firefox cross origin images A:

I could be wrong, but in my experience FabricJS does not set the crossOrigin attribute. In my app, I'm setting this manually. But maybe I'm doing it wrong...

One other thought is that I believe the attribute is case sensitive - the 'O' should be capitalized. In your example above it is all lower case.

Mozilla (the maker of Firefox) has a very detailed explanation on how to use this as well. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/CORS_enabled_image

Lastly, as has been said elsewhere, including the point @andrew is highlighting, the domain that serves the image needs to set the Access-Control-Allow-Origin header. If this is not set by the server that hosts the image, your canvas will always be tainted. If you control that server, then follow @andrew's suggestion (for Apache) or other examples for other server platforms and ensure the header is set. You can verify it is set via the network panel of the developer tools or a packet sniffer.

Please let us know what you find to be the solution to this - CORS can be tricky and confusing, particularly in Fabric and Canvas, and more solutions on the web to the solutions is very helpful to those that need some guidance.

Q: Cannot deserialize value of type `java.lang.String` from Object value (token `JsonToken.START_OBJECT`) A:

You are right about the library not being able to deserialize object into String. You could solve the issue in the following ways:

  • If you expect an arbitrary object in propertiesJson property you could make it of type Map<String, Object> in your ConfigurationProperties class.

  • If propertiesJson can be of any type(like number, string, array, object) you could make it of type Object. In such case ObjectMapper would deserialize the value into an object of the json type's respective counterpart in Java.

Q: getting streaming stopped, reason not-negotiated (-4) error A:

There seems to be an error in the initial part of your pipeline

appsrc (...) caps=image/jpeg,framerate=(fraction)30/1 ! videoconvert

Your appsrc element seems to be outputting a motion JPEG stream and trying to feed that to the videoconvert element, which only takes a raw video stream as input. Probably this can be just solved by putting a decodebin inbetween, which will decode the JPEG frames for you.

Q: How does NPM v7 access the private SSH key without credentials when pulling down private git packages? A:

Check first your dependencie URL: if it is git+https://, it would not prompt for SSH private key passphrase or SSH agent, but would rely on Git credential caching.

Similarily, for SSH URL, check your git config -l for any insteadOf directive

cd /path/to/repo
git config -l --show-scope --show-origin|grep -i insteadof

If an SSH URL is automatically transformed into HTTPS, again SSH agent would not be involved. There was even npm/cli/issue 2610 complaining that SSH is used when HTTPS is specified.

The OP Mark Miretsky explains in the comments:

In fact, it turned out that my SSH URL was being automatically transformed into HTTPS, and, because I had my HTTPS credentials stored in Git Credential Store, it wasn't prompting me for credentials

See also a possible workaround at the end of "Error in initiating Astro after choosing a framework".

Update June 2026: npm/cli#2610, mentioned above as an example of npm using SSH when HTTPS was specified, is now closed. The fix was merged through npm/cli#8703 and released in npm v12.0.0-pre.1. It preserves explicit https://... and git+https://... Git specs instead of rewriting them to git+ssh://git@github.com/....

That evolution does not change the main point of this answer. If there is no SSH passphrase prompt, first check whether SSH is actually being used. A Git insteadOf rule, or a stored HTTPS credential in Git Credential Manager / Git Credential Store, can still make a dependency resolve over HTTPS instead of SSH.

So the git config check remains useful:

git config -l --show-scope --show-origin | grep -i insteadof

The resolved status of npm/cli#2610 only means that newer npm versions containing the fix should no longer perform the opposite rewrite, from explicit HTTPS to SSH.

Q: Powershell generating unknown character when echoing to file A:

tl;dr:

  • In Windows PowerShell, the legacy, ships-with-Windows edition, > and >> create "Unicode" (UTF-16LE) files by default, which invariably use a BOM (byte order mark) at the start of the file and encode each character (Unicode code point) as two bytes (with ASCII-range characters having a NUL (0x0) byte as the first one), which is the source of your problem (most CLIs do not understand this encoding).

    • Note that this is no longer a problem in PowerShell (Core) 7, the modern, cross-platform, install-on-demand edition, at least with ASCII content, as it consistently defaults to BOM-less UTF-8.
      If a different encoding for non-ASCII characters is required, use Set-Content and Add-Content rather than > and >>, with an -Encoding argument.

  • If your file content comprises:

    • ASCII characters only: You can use the Set-Content and Add-Content cmdlets instead of the redirection operators > and >>: these cmdlets default to the ANSI code page determined by the active legacy system locale, of which ASCII is a subset.

    • Non-ASCII characters (too): Use an -Encoding argument to produce the expected encoding; with -Encoding utf8, the pitfall in Windows PowerShell is that you'll invariably create UTF-8 files with BOM, and many CLIs do not recognize such a BOM and treat it as part of the file's content.

      • See below for a workaround for creating BOM-less UTF-8 files in Windows PowerShell.

Systematic overview:

  • In the modern, cross-platform PowerShell (Core) 7 edition (v6 and above), it is now fine to use > and >> as they now create BOM-less UTF-8 files (as all file-writing cmdlets now do consistently).

    • Given that many modern programs expect this character encoding, your code will likely work as-is.
    • If you need a different encoding, call a cmdlet with -Encoding, as discussed next.

  • In the legacy Windows PowerShell edition (whose latest and final version is v5.1), > and >> default to UTF-16LE (which PowerShell incorrectly calls Unicode), which few external programs understand, and which is the cause of your problem.[1]

    • > and >> are in effect alias of Out-File and Out-File -Append, and specifying a different encoding requires calling them explicitly with an -Encoding argument.
      While you can use the $PSDefaultParameterValues preference variable to preset this argument to UTF-8 (e.g., $PSDefaultParameterValues['*:Encoding'] = 'utf8'), note that in Windows PowerShell you'll invariably end up with UTF-8 files with a BOM.

    • However, with string input, you may use Set-Content and Add-Content, which default to Default, representing the system's active ANSI code page, such as Windows-1252 on US-English systems.

      # `-Encoding Default` implied.
# OK with ASCII-only characters, otherwise only if the program
# expects ANSI encoding.
# If you use -Encoding ASCII, any non-ASCII characters become
# *literal ?* chars., i.e. information is *lost*.
# (That can also happen for `-Encoding Default` for Unicode chars.
# outside the character set of the active ANSI code page.)
'#Generated' | Set-Content psftp.scp
'put test.txt' | Add-Content psftp.scp
'quit' | Add-Content psftp.scp

    • It gets tricky if you want BOM-less UTF-8, because Windows PowerShell's cmdlets do not support creating such files - -Encoding utf8 invariably creates files with a BOM (unlike in PowerShell (Core), where you conversely must use -Encoding utf8bom to explicitly request a BOM). Curiously, New-Item does create BOM-less UTF-8 files, so it can be used to create the file, which allows subsequent Add-Content calls to use -Encoding utf8 safely, because they won't add a BOM to existing file content.[2]

      # New-Item, curiously, creates BOM-less UTF-8 files.
# The string must be passed via -Value (or as a *single* pipeline input), 
# and a trailing newline must be added explicitly.
$null = New-Item -Force psftp.scp -Value "#Génerated`n"
'put test.txt' | Add-Content -Encoding utf8 psftp.scp
'quit' | Add-Content -Encoding utf8 psftp.scp

[1] UTF-16LE files created by PowerShell always have a BOM (Byte Order Mark, which is the 2-byte sequence 0xFF, 0xFE, and characters / surrogate-pair halves are represented as 16-bit code units, i.e. as two bytes, with ASCII-range characters having 0x0 (NUL) as the second byte in their two-byte sequence.

[2] If you use Add-Content without an -Encoding argument, it tries to match the existing content of the target file, albeit solely based on the presence of a BOM, if any. In the absence of a BOM, it defaults to the active ANSI code page, like Set-Content, so that a BOM-less UTF-8 file could get corrupted.
